claim: Developmental dyslexia affects approximately 5-10% of individuals in alphabetic writing systems (e.g. English and German).
source: DD affects a large number of individuals across writing systems, and the prevalence is about 5–10% in alphabetic writing systems (e.g. English and German) (Döhla and Heim, 2015; Katusic et al., 2001; Shaywitz, 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Döhla and Heim, 2015; Katusic et al., 2001; Shaywitz, 1996) that provide prevalence data.

claim: Developmental dyslexia affects approximately 4-7% of individuals in morpho-syllabic writing systems (e.g. Chinese and Japanese Kanji).
source: the prevalence is about 5–10% in alphabetic writing systems (e.g. English and German) (Döhla and Heim, 2015; Katusic et al., 2001; Shaywitz, 1996) and about 4–7% in morpho-syllabic writing systems (e.g. Chinese and Japanese Kanji) (Sun et al., 2013; Uno et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Sun et al., 2013; Uno et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2016) that provide prevalence data for morpho-syllabic writing systems.

claim: Phonological deficit has been well-documented across languages in individuals with developmental dyslexia.
source: Multiple deficits have been identified to be associated with DD (Ring and Black, 2018), among which phonological deficit has been well-documented across languages (Gu and Bi, 2020; Snowling and Melby-Lervag, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Gu and Bi, 2020; Snowling and Melby-Lervag, 2016) that document phonological deficits across languages.

claim: Individuals with developmental dyslexia show deficient phonological ability including phonological representation, manipulation, and retrieval even when compared to reading-level controls.
source: Individuals with DD show deficient phonological ability including phonological representation, manipulation, and retrieval even when compared to reading-level controls (Melby-Lervag et al., 2012; Parrila et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Melby-Lervag et al., 2012; Parrila et al., 2020) that compared individuals with DD to reading-level controls.

claim: Phonological deficit in English is associated with lower accuracy in phonological decoding.
source: For example, phonological deficit in English is associated with lower accuracy in phonological decoding (Landerl et al., 1997; Ziegler et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Landerl et al., 1997; Ziegler et al., 2003) that examined phonological decoding accuracy in English.

claim: Phonological deficit in transparent orthographies is associated with slower reading speed with relatively intact accuracy in phonological decoding.
source: it is associated with slower reading speed in transparent orthographies with relatively intact accuracy in phonological decoding (Wimmer and Schurz, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Wimmer and Schurz, 2010) that examined reading speed in transparent orthographies.

claim: In Chinese, phonological deficit is associated with a higher rate of semantic errors during character reading.
source: In Chinese, phonological deficit is associated with a higher rate of semantic errors during character reading (Shu et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Shu et al., 2005) that examined semantic errors in Chinese character reading.

claim: Children with developmental dyslexia over-rely on the semantic cue in Chinese characters during reading due to the inability to use the phonological cue.
source: because children with DD over-rely on the semantic cue in the character during reading due to the inability to use the phonological cue
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the previous statement about semantic errors in Chinese reading and the structure of Chinese characters.

claim: 80% of Chinese characters have a semantic radical and a phonetic radical providing semantic cues and phonological cues of the character, respectively.
source: According to research, 80% of Chinese characters have a semantic radical and a phonetic radical providing semantic cues and phonological cues of the character, respectively (Honorof and Feldman, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Honorof and Feldman, 2006) that provides data on the structure of Chinese characters.

claim: The reading network in the left hemisphere has often been found to show alterations in individuals with developmental dyslexia.
source: At the neurological level, the reading network in the left hemisphere has often been found to show alterations in individuals with DD (Pugh et al., 2000; Richlan, 2012; Richlan, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Pugh et al., 2000; Richlan, 2012; Richlan, 2014) that examined brain alterations in DD.

claim: The reading network alterations in developmental dyslexia include the temporoparietal cortex, the occipitotemporal cortex, and the inferior frontal cortex.
source: the reading network in the left hemisphere has often been found to show alterations in individuals with DD (Pugh et al., 2000; Richlan, 2012; Richlan, 2014), including the temporoparietal cortex (TP), the occipitotemporal cortex (OT), and the inferior frontal cortex
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Pugh et al., 2000; Richlan, 2012; Richlan, 2014) that identified specific brain regions showing alterations.

claim: The left posterior superior temporal gyrus is involved in fine phonological analysis.
source: The left TP area is further subdivided into the posterior superior temporal gyrus (STG), which is involved in fine phonological analysis (Petersen and Fiez, 1993; Richlan, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Petersen and Fiez, 1993; Richlan, 2012) that examined the function of the posterior STG.

claim: The inferior parietal lobule is associated with general attention control.
source: the inferior parietal lobule (IPL) which is associated with general attention control (Richlan, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Richlan, 2014) that examined the function of the IPL.

claim: The temporoparietal region tends to show reduced brain activation in individuals with developmental dyslexia in alphabetic languages.
source: This TP region tends to show reduced brain activation in individuals with DD in alphabetic languages as demonstrated in a cross-linguistic study of English, Italian, and French (Paulesu et al., 2001) and several meta-analysis studies in alphabetic languages (Maisog et al., 2008; Martin et al., 2016; Paulesu et al., 2014; Richlan et al., 2009; Richlan et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies including a cross-linguistic study (Paulesu et al., 2001) and meta-analyses (Maisog et al., 2008; Martin et al., 2016; Paulesu et al., 2014; Richlan et al., 2009; Richlan et al., 2011).

claim: The left occipitotemporal area has been consistently found to show reduced activation in individuals with developmental dyslexia across morpho-syllabic and alphabetic languages.
source: The left OT area, including the middle occipital gyrus (MOG), inferior temporal gyrus (ITG) and fusiform gyrus, has been consistently found to show reduced activation in individuals with DD across morpho-syllabic and alphabetic languages (Bolger et al., 2008; Cao et al., 2020; Centanni et al., 2019; Chyl et al., 2019; Paz-Alonso et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bolger et al., 2008; Cao et al., 2020; Centanni et al., 2019; Chyl et al., 2019; Paz-Alonso et al., 2018) that examined activation in the OT area across languages.

claim: The left occipitotemporal region is associated with visuo-orthographic processing during reading.
source: This region is associated with visuo-orthographic processing during reading (Glezer et al., 2016; Glezer et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Glezer et al., 2016; Glezer et al., 2019) that examined the function of the OT region.

claim: The precentral gyrus may relate to compensatory articulatory processes in dyslexia.
source: The precentral gyrus may relate to compensatory articulatory processes in dyslexia (Hancock et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Hancock et al., 2017) that examined the role of the precentral gyrus in dyslexia.

claim: The inferior frontal gyrus has been known to be involved in phonological and semantic retrieval, lexical selection and integration.
source: whereas the IFG has been known to be involved in phonological and semantic retrieval, lexical selection and integration (Booth et al., 2007a; Booth et al., 2007b; Costafreda et al., 2006; Szatkowska et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Booth et al., 2007a; Booth et al., 2007b; Costafreda et al., 2006; Szatkowska et al., 2000) that examined IFG function.

claim: Reduced activation in the left inferior frontal gyrus was confirmed by many fMRI studies and meta-analysis studies.
source: Although reduced activation in the left IFG was confirmed by many fMRI studies and meta-analysis studies (Booth et al., 2007a; Cao et al., 2006; Richlan et al., 2010; Wimmer et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple fMRI and meta-analysis studies (Booth et al., 2007a; Cao et al., 2006; Richlan et al., 2010; Wimmer et al., 2010).

claim: Increased activation in the left inferior frontal gyrus was also reported in many fMRI studies.
source: increased activation in the left IFG was also reported in many fMRI studies (Grunling et al., 2004; Kronbichler et al., 2006; Waldie et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple fMRI studies (Grunling et al., 2004; Kronbichler et al., 2006; Waldie et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2010).

claim: Inconsistent results regarding left IFG activation may be related to task and task difficulty.
source: The inconsistent results may be related to task and task difficulty (Waldie et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Waldie et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2010) that examined task effects on IFG activation.

claim: Inconsistent results regarding left IFG activation may be related to orthographic transparency.
source: The inconsistent results may be related to task and task difficulty (Waldie et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2010), orthographic transparency (Martin et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Martin et al., 2016) that examined orthographic transparency effects.

claim: Inconsistent results regarding left IFG activation may be related to age of participants.
source: The inconsistent results may be related to task and task difficulty (Waldie et al., 2013; Wimmer et al., 2010), orthographic transparency (Martin et al., 2016), and age of participants (Chyl et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Chyl et al., 2019) that examined age effects on IFG activation.

claim: Readers with developmental dyslexia in English, Italian, and French showed similar brain abnormality during an explicit word reading task and an implicit reading task.
source: Paulesu et al., 2001 found that readers with DD in English, Italian, and French showed similar brain abnormality during an explicit word reading task and an implicit reading task
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a specific study (Paulesu et al., 2001) that examined cross-linguistic brain abnormalities.

claim: Chinese and English children with developmental dyslexia showed language-universal deficits.
source: Hu et al., 2010 found that Chinese and English children with DD showed language-universal deficits
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Hu et al., 2010) that compared Chinese and English children with DD.

claim: Children with developmental dyslexia in both Chinese and French showed common reduction of brain activation in the left fusiform gyrus and superior temporal gyrus.
source: Feng et al., 2020 found that children with DD in both Chinese and French showed common reduction of brain activation in the left fusiform gyrus and STG
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Feng et al., 2020) that compared Chinese and French children with DD.

claim: Functional abnormalities in the brain vary with orthographic depth in alphabetic languages.
source: In a meta-analysis study (Martin et al., 2016), researchers directly compared brain deficits associated with DD between transparent and opaque orthographies and found that functional abnormalities in the brain vary with orthographic depth in alphabetic languages
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis study (Martin et al., 2016) that examined orthographic depth effects.

claim: Consistent reduction of brain activation was found in a left occipitotemporal area regardless of orthographic depth.
source: Specifically, consistent reduction of brain activation was found in a left OT area regardless of orthographic depth
evidence: The claim is based on findings from the Martin et al., 2016 meta-analysis study mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Greater reduction in brain activation was found in the left fusiform gyrus, left temporoparietal cortex and left IFG pars orbitalis in transparent orthographies than in opaque orthographies.
source: whereas greater reduction was found in the left fusiform gyrus, left TP and left IFG pars orbitalis in transparent orthographies than in opaque orthographies
evidence: The claim is based on findings from the Martin et al., 2016 meta-analysis study mentioned in the context.

claim: Greater reduction in brain activation was found in the bilateral intraparietal sulcus, left precuneus and left IFG pars triangularis in opaque orthographies than in transparent orthographies.
source: and greater reduction in the bilateral intraparietal sulcus, left precuneus and left IFG pars triangularis was found in opaque orthographies than in transparent orthographies
evidence: The claim is based on findings from the Martin et al., 2016 meta-analysis study mentioned in the context.

claim: Chinese-English bilingual children with developmental dyslexia showed both language-universal and language-specific deficits for Chinese and English.
source: In a recent study on Chinese-English bilingual children with DD, researchers also found both language-universal and language-specific deficits for Chinese and English (Cao et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Cao et al., 2020) that examined bilingual children with DD.

claim: Language-universal deficits might be related to the causal risk of developmental dyslexia while language-specific deficits tend to be interpreted as a result of interaction between DD and the specific language system that one studies.
source: The language-universal deficits might be related to the causal risk of DD while the language-specific deficits tend to be interpreted as a result of interaction between DD and the specific language system that one studies
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pattern of findings across studies and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: Significant alteration in the left middle frontal gyrus or dorsal IFG has been consistently reported in different studies on developmental dyslexia in Chinese.
source: Significant alteration in the left middle frontal gyrus (MFG) or dorsal IFG has been consistently reported in different studies (Cao et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013a; Siok et al., 2004; Siok et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Cao et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013a; Siok et al., 2004; Siok et al., 2008) on Chinese DD.

claim: Alteration in the left temporoparietal areas has been reported in only a few studies on developmental dyslexia in Chinese.
source: while the alteration in the left TP areas has been reported in only a few studies (Cao et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to a limited number of studies (Cao et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2010) on Chinese DD.

claim: The left dorsal IFG is more involved in Chinese reading than in English reading in typical readers.
source: It has been found that the left dorsal IFG is more involved in Chinese reading than in English reading, while the left TP is more involved in English reading than in Chinese reading in typical readers (Bolger et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Bolger et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2005) that compared Chinese and English reading in typical readers.

claim: The left temporoparietal cortex is more involved in English reading than in Chinese reading in typical readers.
source: It has been found that the left dorsal IFG is more involved in Chinese reading than in English reading, while the left TP is more involved in English reading than in Chinese reading in typical readers (Bolger et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Bolger et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2005) that compared Chinese and English reading in typical readers.

claim: Previous meta-analysis studies on alphabetic languages have found grey matter reduction in the left temporoparietal area.
source: Previous meta-analysis studies on alphabetic languages have found grey matter reduction in the left TP area (Linkersdörfer et al., 2012; McGrath and Stoodley, 2019; Richlan et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple meta-analysis studies (Linkersdörfer et al., 2012; McGrath and Stoodley, 2019; Richlan et al., 2013).

claim: Previous meta-analysis studies on alphabetic languages have found grey matter reduction in the left occipitotemporal area.
source: as well as the left OT area (Linkersdörfer et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis study (Linkersdörfer et al., 2012).

claim: Studies on morpho-syllabic languages have found grey matter reduction within the classic reading network.
source: In consistent, studies on morpho-syllabic languages have also found grey matter reduction within the classic reading network (Liu et al., 2013b; Siok et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Liu et al., 2013b; Siok et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2016) on morpho-syllabic languages.

claim: Studies have found abnormal brain structures outside the classic reading network in developmental dyslexia, for example, in putamen, cerebellum, thalamus, and caudate.
source: However, there are also studies that found abnormal brain structures outside the classic reading network, for example, in putamen, cerebellum, thalamus, and caudate etc. (Adrian-Ventura et al., 2020; Brambati et al., 2004; Brown et al., 2001; Jagger-Rickels et al., 2018; Jednorog et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Adrian-Ventura et al., 2020; Brambati et al., 2004; Brown et al., 2001; Jagger-Rickels et al., 2018; Jednorog et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Learning a specific language with developmental dyslexia may affect brain development in regions that are specifically important for that language and related functions.
source: Learning a specific language with DD may affect brain development in regions that are specifically important for that language and related functions (Mechelli et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Mechelli et al., 2004) that examined language effects on brain development.

claim: Researchers found reduced GMV and brain activation in the left middle frontal gyrus in Chinese children with developmental dyslexia.
source: In a study by Siok et al., 2008, researchers examined both structural and functional alterations in Chinese children with DD, and found reduced GMV and brain activation in the left MFG
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a specific study (Siok et al., 2008) that examined both structural and functional alterations.

claim: A study located a key region in the left inferior parietal lobule, which showed reduced GMV and activation in English-speaking readers with developmental dyslexia.
source: Another study located a key region in the left IPL, which showed reduced GMV and activation in English-speaking readers with DD (Hoeft et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Hoeft et al., 2007) that examined the left IPL in English-speaking readers with DD.

claim: A recent study found a dissociation between brain structural development and brain functional development in some brain regions (e.g. left fusiform gyrus) in the context of reading development.
source: A recent study, from a developmental perspective, found a dissociation between brain structural development and brain functional development in some brain regions (e.g. left fusiform gyrus) in the context of reading development (Siok et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Siok et al., 2020) that examined developmental changes in brain structure and function.

claim: Learning experience may significantly shape brain function independent of brain structure.
source: suggesting that learning experience may significantly shape brain function independent of brain structure
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings of the Siok et al., 2020 study mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: For the functional studies, a total of 2728 participants (controls:1370, DD:1358) were included.
source: For the functional studies, a total of 2728 participants (controls:1370, DD:1358) were included
evidence: The claim is based on data extracted from the included studies as reported in the manuscript.

claim: The mean age was 16.56 years for controls and 16.26 years for participants with DD in functional studies.
source: and the mean age was 16.56 years for controls and 16.26 years for participants with DD
evidence: The claim is based on data extracted from the included studies as reported in the manuscript.

claim: There were 79 functional experiments in alphabetic languages.
source: Specifically, there were 79 functional experiments in alphabetic languages
evidence: The claim is based on data from the literature search and study selection process.

claim: There were 12 functional experiments in morpho-syllabic languages.
source: There were 12 functional experiments in morpho-syllabic languages
evidence: The claim is based on data from the literature search and study selection process.

claim: In the meta-analysis of functional studies in alphabetic languages, hypoactivation in DD was found in a large cluster peaked at the left supramarginal gyrus which extended to the inferior frontal cortex, occipitotemporal cortex and cerebellum.
source: In the meta-analysis of functional studies in alphabetic languages, hypoactivation in DD was found in a large cluster peaked at the left supramarginal gyrus which extended to the inferior frontal cortex, occipitotemporal cortex and cerebellum, a cluster peaked at the right MOG and a cluster peaked at right STG (Table 1 and Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1A.

claim: Hyperactivation in DD was found in the right cerebellum and bilateral caudate nucleus in alphabetic languages.
source: Hyperactivation in DD was found in the right cerebellum and bilateral caudate nucleus
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: In the meta-analysis of functional studies in morpho-syllabic languages, hypoactivation in DD was found in left IFG opercular part, left supramarginal gyrus and left ITG.
source: In the meta-analysis of functional studies in morpho-syllabic languages, hypoactivation in DD was found in left IFG opercular part, left supramarginal gyrus and left ITG
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Hyperactivation in DD was found in right precentral gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus in morpho-syllabic languages.
source: Hyperactivation in DD was found in right precentral gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) (Table 2, Table 3 and Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Tables 2, 3 and Figure 1C.

claim: In the meta-analysis of structural studies in alphabetic languages, readers with DD showed a decrease in GMV in the left IFG orbital part, right STG and right caudate nucleus.
source: In the meta-analysis of structural studies in alphabetic languages, readers with DD showed a decrease in GMV in the left IFG orbital part, right STG and right caudate nucleus (Table 2 and Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Table 2 and Figure 1B.

claim: Readers with DD showed an increase in GMV in the left IPL and right MTG in alphabetic languages.
source: In contrast, readers with DD showed an increase in GMV in the left IPL and right MTG
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: In the meta-analysis of structural studies in morpho-syllabic languages, readers with DD showed a decrease in GMV in the left temporoparietal cortex, left calcarine cortex and left MFG.
source: In the meta-analysis of structural studies in morpho-syllabic languages, readers with DD showed a decrease in GMV in the left temporoparietal cortex, left calcarine cortex and left MFG
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Readers with DD showed an increase in GMV in the right STG in morpho-syllabic languages.
source: Readers with DD showed an increase in GMV in the right STG (Table 4 and Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Table 4 and Figure 1D.

claim: Greater reduction of brain activation in alphabetic languages than in morpho-syllabic languages was found in the left MTG, right STG and left fusiform gyrus.
source: For the direct comparison between the morpho-syllabic and alphabetic groups in functional studies, we found greater reduction of brain activation in alphabetic languages than in morpho-syllabic languages in the left MTG, right STG and left fusiform gyrus
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the direct comparison analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Greater reduction of brain activation in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages was found in the left IFG, opercular part.
source: We found greater reduction of brain activation in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages in the left IFG, opercular part
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the direct comparison analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Greater increase of brain activation in DD in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages was found in the right precentral gyrus.
source: and greater increase of brain activation in DD in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages in the right precentral gyrus (Table 5, Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the direct comparison analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Table 5 and Figure 2A.

claim: Greater reduction of GMV in DD in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages was found in the left STG, left IFG opercular part, left MFG, left supramarginal gyrus, left superior occipital gyrus and left insula.
source: For the direct comparison between the morpho-syllabic and alphabetic groups in structural studies, we found greater reduction of GMV in DD in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages in the left STG, left IFG opercular part, left MFG, left supramarginal gyrus, left superior occipital gyrus (SOG) and left insula
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the direct comparison analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Greater increase of GMV in DD in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages was found in the right STG and left ITG.
source: We also found greater increase of GMV in DD in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages in the right STG and left ITG (Table 6, Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the direct comparison analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Table 6 and Figure 2B.

claim: Conjunction analysis between the language differences in structural studies and functional studies produced an overlap of 377 voxels in the left IFG opercular part.
source: To identify the common language differences between the structural and functional studies, we conducted a conjunction analysis between the language differences in structural studies and functional studies. This produced an overlap of 377 voxels in the left IFG opercular part, with a peak at (–52, 10, 24)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the conjunction analysis conducted in this study.

claim: The left IFG opercular part showed greater reduction of both GMV and brain activation in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages.
source: indicating greater reduction of both GMV and brain activation in morpho-syllabic languages than in alphabetic languages (Figure 2C)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the conjunction analysis, with data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Multimodal meta-analysis in alphabetic languages showed that decreased GMV and hypoactivation in DD were found in the bilateral STG and left IFG triangular part.
source: Multimodal meta-analysis in alphabetic languages showed that decreased GMV and hypoactivation in DD were found in the bilateral STG and left IFG triangular part
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the multimodal meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Increased GMV and hypoactivation in DD were found in left IPL and left cerebellum in alphabetic languages.
source: increased GMV and hypoactivation in DD were found in left IPL and left cerebellum
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the multimodal meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Decreased GMV and hyperactivation in DD were found in bilateral caudate and right cerebellum in alphabetic languages.
source: decreased GMV and hyperactivation in DD were found in bilateral caudate and right cerebellum (Table 7, Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the multimodal meta-analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Table 7 and Figure 3A.

claim: Multimodal meta-analysis in morpho-syllabic languages showed that decreased GMV and hypoactivation in DD were found in the left STG and left IFG opercular part.
source: Multimodal meta-analysis in morpho-syllabic languages showed that decreased GMV and hypoactivation in DD were found in the left STG and left IFG opercular part
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the multimodal meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Increased GMV and hyperactivation in DD were found in the right MTG in morpho-syllabic languages.
source: increased GMV and hyperactivation in DD were found in the right MTG
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the multimodal meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Decreased GMV and hyperactivation in DD were found in left STG in morpho-syllabic languages.
source: decreased GMV and hyperactivation in DD were found in left STG
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the multimodal meta-analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Conjunction analysis of the multimodal maps produced an overlap of 482 voxels in the left STG, indicating shared reduction of GMV and hypoactivation in both types of writing systems.
source: To identify the common multimodal deficits in alphabetic languages and morpho-syllabic languages, we conducted a conjunction analysis of the thresholded multimodal maps of the two types of writing systems. This procedure produced an overlap of 482 voxels in the left STG, which peaked at (−54,–34, 20), indicating shared reduction of GMV and hypoactivation in both types of writing systems (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the conjunction analysis conducted in this study, with data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Convergent structural and functional deficit was found in the left STG due to reduced GMV and brain activation in both alphabetic languages and morpho-syllabic languages.
source: Across writing systems, convergent structural and functional deficit was found in the left STG due to reduced GMV and brain activation in both alphabetic languages and morpho-syllabic languages
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the multimodal and conjunction analyses conducted in this study.

claim: The left STG is a very important component in the language network.
source: The left STG is a very important component in the language network (Friederici, 2012; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Friederici, 2012; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007) that examined the role of the left STG in language.

claim: The left STG is a key region in the reading network.
source: as well a key region in the reading network (Pugh et al., 2000; Richlan, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Pugh et al., 2000; Richlan, 2014) that examined the role of the left STG in reading.

claim: The left STG is involved in phonological representation and phonological processing during both spoken language processing and reading.
source: It is involved in phonological representation and phonological processing during both spoken language processing and reading (Bolger et al., 2005; Enge et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Bolger et al., 2005; Enge et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2005) that examined the function of the left STG.

claim: Proficient reading is characterized by convergence between speech and print at the left STG regardless of languages.
source: Recent research has suggested that proficient reading is characterized by convergence between speech and print at this region regardless of languages, as multivariate brain activity patterns are similar for speech and print at this region (Chyl et al., 2021)
